strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching problem with a sensible strategy: identify problematic seam regions, repair their alignment locally, and reconnect the seam. This can resolve structural discontinuities that seam relocation alone cannot fix.

Figures 1, 7, 10, and 11 demonstrate useful visual improvements, particularly on curbs and stairs. Quantitative evaluation covers 79 image pairs across three datasets, including two public collections.

The reported CPU timings and user study support practical promise. The proposed method receives 108 of 160 first-place votes on the eight selected examples and avoids the substantial runtime of the iterative baseline [17] in many cases.
The high-level pipeline is understandable, borrowed methods and public data sources are cited, and Section 4.4 provides a meaningful limitation discussion with a concrete failure example.
weaknesses: The technical advance over existing seam-quality evaluation [17] and seam-guided alignment [18] is insufficiently isolated. Quantitative comparisons include only seam-cutting methods [16,17], while [18,26] receive selected qualitative comparisons. Beyond Figure 4's single illustrative example, controlled ablations of patch selection, flow tapering, and merging constraints are missing. Only one initial alignment method and one initial seam method are tested, leaving the claimed general applicability empirically unverified.

The central flow modification is underspecified. Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid of spatial position, while the text applies f to a displacement vector without explicitly defining the resulting vector warp. Taper orientation for general seams, treatment of overlapping repair patches, and continuity around the full patch boundary are unclear. Fixing boundary labels in Section 3.5 does not itself guarantee continuity of warped image content. These details matter for reproducing the proposed contribution.

The claim that the method can almost remove the rough-alignment assumption exceeds its demonstrated scope. Section 3.4 assumes small residual parallax within patches, and Section 4.4 requires an initially mostly successful seam. Furthermore, the criterion max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) accepts uniformly high-error seams, so it cannot establish absolute seam quality. The contribution should be scoped more precisely to local residual repair, with evidence showing sensitivity to initial alignment quality.

Independent perceptual validation remains limited. Equation (5) averages the same SSIM signal used to identify repair regions and does not directly measure geometric distortion away from the seam. The manuscript itself reports disagreement between this metric and visual quality on SEAGULL pair 17. The complementary user study uses only eight manually selected 'controversial' examples, without sufficiently specified selection criteria, presentation randomization, or uncertainty estimates, limiting generalization of its favorable result.

A minor reporting inconsistency needs correction: Table 1 contains 159 rankings for [17] and 161 for [16], although 20 participants ranking eight groups should yield 160 rankings per method. This does not overturn the proposed method's reported preference advantage, but the counts should be reconciled.
